questions.question: What does the intensified Arabic word 'zilzal' in the opening verse convey about the earthquake of the Last Day?
options: A localized seismic tremor confined to a single region
Extreme, repeated, and total shaking of the entire planet
A symbolic spiritual upheaval rather than a physical event
A gradual disturbance that allows time for evacuation
questions.explanation: Layer 1 explains that 'zilzal' is an intensified form conveying extreme, repeated, and total shaking, unlike any earthquake known to human experience. It is not a localized tremor but a complete upheaval of the planet at the onset of the Day of Judgment.

questions.question: True or false: The 'athqal' (burdens) that the earth will discharge are understood by classical scholars to include the dead bodies buried within it as well as treasures hidden in its depths.
questions.explanation: Layer 1 identifies the burdens primarily as the dead buried within the earth who will be expelled at the resurrection, and notes that some commentators also include hidden treasures of gold, silver, and precious minerals which the earth will throw out, exposing all worldly wealth.

questions.question: Which hadith from Abu Hurairah, cited by Imam Tabari and Ibn Kathir, explains the meaning of the earth 'narrating its news' in verse 4?
options: The Prophet said the earth will praise Allah on that Day with a tongue given to it
The Prophet said the earth will testify against every male and female servant about everything they did upon its back
The Prophet said the earth will release its waters and rivers as final witnesses
The Prophet said the earth will collapse silently without giving any testimony
questions.explanation: According to layer 2, Imam Tabari and Ibn Kathir cite the hadith of Abu Hurairah in which the Prophet explained that the earth's 'news' is that it will testify against every male and female servant, saying 'He did this on such and such a day, and she did this on such and such a day.'

questions.question: True or false: According to classical scholars like Tabari, the verb 'awha' used for Allah's command to the earth is the same verb used elsewhere in the Quran for divine revelation to prophets and for the instinctive guidance given to bees.
questions.explanation: Layer 2 notes that Tabari explains 'awha laha' as Allah's direct command, employing the same verb used for revelation to prophets and for inspiring instinctive behavior in animals like bees as mentioned in Surah Al-Nahl. It conveys precise, direct, and hidden communication that cannot be disobeyed.

questions.question: How does Sayyid Qutb in Fi Zilal al-Quran interpret the word 'ashtatan' (in scattered groups) in verse 6?
options: As a reference to the geographic dispersion of nations across the earth
As proof that resurrection occurs in stages over many days
As a moment when superficial worldly bonds dissolve and the only meaningful division is between those who obeyed Allah and those who did not
As an indication that families will remain united as single groups
questions.explanation: Layer 3 explains that Sayyid Qutb sees 'ashtatan' as dissolving every human pretension of social cohesion. Families, nations, tribes and civilizations that thought themselves unified will discover that the deeper division is between those who obeyed Allah and those who did not.

questions.question: What lesson does Wahbah al-Zuhayli draw from verses 7 and 8 in Al-Tafsir al-Munir?
options: Only major sins and major good deeds are weighed; minor ones are forgiven automatically
These verses establish a moral universe of absolute precision where no deed exists in a moral vacuum
Reward and punishment are random expressions of divine will rather than precise accounting
The atom's weight refers exclusively to acts of formal worship
questions.explanation: Layer 3 reports that Wahbah al-Zuhayli sees verses 7 and 8 as the ethical climax of the surah, establishing a moral universe of absolute precision. He connects this to the Prophet's saying 'la tahqiranna min al-ma'ruf shay'an' (do not belittle any good deed), emphasizing that small goods and small evils both register fully with Allah.

questions.question: True or false: A Bedouin who heard verses 7 and 8 said 'this is enough for me,' and the Prophet praised him by saying 'he has become a faqih.'
questions.explanation: Layer 1 narrates this famous incident: a Bedouin who heard the Prophet recite verses 7 and 8 said, 'This is enough for me.' The Prophet praised him saying, 'He has become a faqih,' meaning a person of deep religious understanding, indicating that these two verses encapsulate a complete moral worldview.
